cards.title: Millions of names, one answer
cards.body:
There are hundreds of millions of domain names. No single computer keeps a list of them all, and no single computer could answer everyone's questions.

Yet a DNS lookup usually takes just a few milliseconds, and often the answer comes back without your question ever leaving your house. How?

cards.title: First stop: memory
cards.body:
Your device keeps recent answers in a **cache**: a short-term memory of lookups it has already done. If you visited example.com a minute ago, the address is probably still there, and no question needs to be sent at all.

If it isn't, your device asks a **resolver**. That's a server whose job is to find answers for you, usually run by your internet provider or by a public DNS service you've chosen. The resolver has its own cache too, shared by everyone who uses it, so popular names are often answered straight away.

cards.title: The resolver's trip
cards.body:
When the resolver doesn't know the answer, it works it out step by step, like asking for directions by country, then town, then street:

1. It asks a **root server**: "Who handles `.com`?" There are 13 named root servers, run as well over a thousand copies around the world.
2. It asks a **`.com` TLD server**: "Who's in charge of `example.com`?"
3. It asks example.com's **authoritative server**, the one that holds example.com's actual records: "What's the address?"

The resolver sends the answer back to your device, and both of them keep a copy in their cache for next time.

cards.prompt: Nobody has looked up example.com recently. Put the steps of the lookup in order.

items.label: Your device checks its own cache
The resolver asks a root server who handles .com
The resolver asks a .com server who's in charge of example.com
The resolver asks example.com's authoritative server for the address
The answer comes back, and copies are kept in the caches

cards.explanation: Your device always checks its **cache** first. Then the resolver goes from general to specific: **root**, then **TLD**, then the **authoritative** server, which is the only one that actually knows example.com's address. Finally, the answer is saved so the next lookup is instant.

cards.prompt: Match each DNS server to its job.

pairs.right: Does the asking for you and caches answers
Knows where to find each TLD's servers
Knows who's in charge of each domain

cards.explanation: The **resolver** works for you. The **root** servers point to the TLD servers, the **TLD** servers point to each domain's authoritative servers, and the **authoritative** server holds the real answer.

cards.prompt: Which server holds the official IP address of example.com?
cards.explanation: Only example.com's **authoritative** server holds its official records. The root and TLD servers just point the way, like signposts. Your device and the resolver may keep *copies* in their caches, but copies come from the authoritative server in the first place.

cards.title: How long to remember: TTL again
cards.body:
A cached answer can't be kept forever, because a website might move to a new address. So every DNS answer comes with a **TTL** in **seconds**: how long it may be kept in a cache before it has to be looked up again. A TTL of 300 means "remember this for 5 minutes".

You've seen the letters TTL before! In Module 3, a packet's **TTL** was a **hop limit**, lowered by 1 at each router. They share a name (*time to live*) but they are **different things**:

- A packet's TTL counts **hops**, and stops lost packets looping forever.
- A DNS answer's TTL counts **seconds**, and decides how long it can be cached.

cards.prompt: A DNS answer has a TTL of **3,600**. How many **minutes** can it be cached for?
cards.explanation: DNS TTLs are in seconds, and there are 60 seconds in a minute, so 3,600 ÷ 60 = **60 minutes**: one hour. If you typed 3,600, that's the number of seconds.

cards.prompt: `dig` is another tool for DNS lookups, and it shows more detail. Run `dig example.com`, then find the **TTL** in the ANSWER SECTION. It's the number just after the name.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up example.com and show the full answer
commands.output:
; <<>> DiG 9.18.28 <<>> example.com
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41253
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 65494
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;example.com.			IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.		1800	IN	A	198.51.100.10

;; Query time: 24 msec
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.53#53(127.0.0.53) (UDP)
;; WHEN: Tue Sep 29 10:14:02 UTC 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 56

success.question: What is the TTL of this answer, in seconds?

cards.explanation: The answer line reads `example.com. 1800 IN A 198.51.100.10`. From left to right, that's the name, the **TTL** (1,800 seconds, which is 30 minutes), the class (`IN`, for internet), the record type (`A`, an address), and the IP address itself. You'll learn about record types in the next lesson.

cards.prompt: At **11:50** you look up a website, and the answer has a TTL of **3,600**. At **12:00** the website moves to a new IP address. By what time can you be sure your device will use the new address?

options.text: Never: the old address is cached forever

cards.explanation:
Your device may keep the old answer for 3,600 seconds (one hour) from when it got it: **11:50 + 1 hour = 12:50**. After that it must look the name up again and gets the new address. It won't happen at 12:00, because nothing tells your cache the site moved. It's also not 13:00, because the hour started when you looked it up, not when the site moved.

TTL is the rule, but in practice some apps and resolvers cache a little differently (for example, a browser may keep its own copy for a short time), so real changes can take slightly longer to reach everyone. That's why website owners often lower the TTL before a move.

cards.prompt: Which statement about the two kinds of TTL is **true**?

options.text: A packet's TTL counts router hops; a DNS answer's TTL counts seconds of caching
They're the same number: the DNS TTL is copied into each packet

cards.explanation: A **packet's** TTL is lowered by 1 at every router, and the packet is dropped at 0. It counts **hops**. A **DNS answer's** TTL says how many **seconds** it may be cached. Same letters, same idea of a limit, but completely separate numbers that are used for different jobs.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Your device checks its **cache** first, then asks a **resolver**.
- The resolver asks a **root server**, then a **TLD server**, then the domain's **authoritative server**, which holds the real answer.
- Answers are cached for their **TTL**, measured in seconds.
- DNS TTL (seconds of caching) is different from a packet's TTL (a hop limit).

Next: the different kinds of answer DNS can give, and how to read them.
